## Teaching points

1. Lemierre syndrome typically strikes healthy adolescents and young adults: pharyngitis, then (often after apparent improvement) rigors, sepsis and septic emboli, usually to the lungs, within about a week.
2. A negative rapid streptococcal test does not exclude Fusobacterium necrophorum pharyngitis.
3. Sepsis with thrombocytopenia, raised bilirubin and multiple nodular or cavitating lung lesions after a recent sore throat should prompt contrast CT of the neck.
4. Treat with antibiotics that reliably cover anaerobes (piperacillin–tazobactam, a carbapenem, or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) and drain any collection; the role of anticoagulation remains unsettled.
5. Septic pulmonary emboli can progress to ARDS within hours.
